Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Context. Swift data are revolutionising our understanding of Gamma Ray Bursts. Since bursts fade rapidly, it is desirable to create and disseminate accurate light curves rapidly.   Aims. To provide the community with an online repository of X-ray light curves obtained with Swift. The light curves should be of the quality expected of published data, but automatically created and updated so as to be self-consistent and rapidly available. Methods. We have produced a suite of programs which automatically generates Swift/XRT light curves of GRBs. Effects of the damage to the CCD, automatic readout-mode switching and pile-up are appropriately handled, and the data are binned with variable bin durations, as necessary for a fading source.   Results. The light curve repository website (http://www.swift.ac.uk/xrt_curves) contains light curves, hardness ratios and deep images for every GRB which Swift's XRT has observed. When new GRBs are detected, light curves are created and updated within minutes of the data arriving at the UK Swift Science Data Centre.

**Context.** Swift data are revolutionising our understanding of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Because bursts fade rapidly, it is essential to generate and disseminate accurate light curves as quickly as possible.  

**Aims.** We aim to provide the community with an online repository of X-ray light curves obtained with Swift. These light curves are intended to meet the quality standards expected of published data, while being generated and updated automatically to ensure self-consistency and rapid availability.  

**Methods.** We have developed a suite of programs that automatically generates Swift/XRT light curves for GRBs. The effects of CCD damage, automatic readout-mode switching, and pile-up are appropriately handled, and the data are binned using variable bin durations, as required for a fading source.  

**Results.** The light curve repository website (http://www.swift.ac.uk/xrt_curves) contains light curves, hardness ratios, and deep images for every GRB observed by Swift’s XRT. When new GRBs are detected, light curves are created and updated within minutes of the data arriving at the UK Swift Science Data Centre.

Swift observations are transforming what we know about gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Because these events dim very quickly, it is important to generate and share reliable light curves as soon as possible.

The goal is to offer researchers an online archive of X-ray light curves produced from Swift observations. These light curves are intended to match the standard expected for published scientific data, while being generated and refreshed automatically to ensure consistency and fast access.

To achieve this, we developed a set of software tools that automatically produce GRB light curves from Swift/XRT data. The system accounts for CCD damage, automatic changes in readout mode, and pile-up effects. It also uses variable time bins when needed, which is appropriate for sources that fade over time.

The resulting light-curve archive, available at http://www.swift.ac.uk/xrt_curves, provides light curves, hardness ratios, and deep images for every GRB observed by Swift’s XRT. For newly discovered GRBs, the light curves are generated and revised within minutes after the data reach the UK Swift Science Data Centre.

Swift data are transforming our understanding of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) by making it possible to produce and share accurate X-ray light curves very rapidly after an event is detected. Because GRBs evolve quickly, especially during their early afterglow phases, timely access to reliable data is essential for interpreting their behaviour and coordinating follow-up observations across the astronomical community.

The aim of this project is to provide an online repository of Swift X-ray light curves that are suitable for direct scientific use. The light curves are designed to be publication-quality, internally self-consistent, and available as quickly as possible. By offering a standardised set of products, the repository allows researchers to compare different bursts more easily and reduces the need for individual teams to repeat the same data-processing steps.

To achieve this, a suite of automated programs has been developed to generate Swift/XRT light curves. These programs account for several instrumental and observational complications that can affect the quality of the data. They handle damage to the CCD, transitions between different readout modes, pile-up in bright sources, and the need for variable time binning as GRB afterglows fade. This automation ensures that the resulting light curves are both robust and produced with minimal delay.

The repository website provides a comprehensive set of data products for every Gamma Ray Burst observed by Swift’s X-Ray Telescope. In addition to X-ray light curves, it includes hardness ratios, which help track spectral changes over time, and deep images that reveal the field around each burst. These resources give researchers a convenient and consistent way to examine the temporal and spectral evolution of GRB afterglows.

New GRB light curves are created and updated within minutes of data arriving at the UK Swift Science Data Centre. As further observations are received, the products are refreshed automatically, ensuring that the repository remains current. This rapid and systematic approach makes the database an important tool for both immediate follow-up work and longer-term studies of Gamma Ray Bursts.
outputs.L4:
Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic and rapidly evolving phenomena in the Universe, and their X-ray afterglows provide crucial information about the physics of the explosion, the surrounding environment, and the central engine that powers the event. Since the launch of the Swift satellite, the X-Ray Telescope (XRT) has played a central role in observing these afterglows, often beginning observations within minutes of the initial burst detection. Because GRB afterglows can fade quickly and show complex temporal behavior, there is a strong need for light curves that are produced rapidly, accurately, and in a consistent manner. Such light curves are essential not only for immediate follow-up decisions, but also for long-term statistical studies of GRB populations.

To meet this need, an automated software pipeline has been developed to generate high-quality Swift/XRT GRB light curves. The pipeline is designed to process XRT data in a uniform and reliable way, producing results that are suitable for scientific analysis and publication. It accounts for the major instrumental and observational effects that can influence XRT data. These include changes in CCD performance caused by damage to the detector, transitions between different XRT readout modes, photon pile-up in bright sources, and the need for variable time binning as the source brightness changes. By correcting for these effects automatically, the system ensures that the resulting light curves are self-consistent and comparable from one burst to another.

The pipeline also adapts to the wide range of count rates observed in GRB afterglows. Early afterglows can be extremely bright, requiring careful treatment of pile-up and rapid time sampling, while later observations may contain only a small number of photons and therefore require wider time bins to achieve useful signal-to-noise. The software handles these changes dynamically, producing light curves that preserve temporal detail where possible while maintaining statistically meaningful measurements at late times.

The results are made available through an online repository containing Swift/XRT products for every GRB observed by the instrument. For each burst, the repository provides calibrated X-ray light curves, hardness ratios, and deep images. These products allow users to examine both the temporal and spectral evolution of GRB afterglows and to identify features such as flares, breaks, plateaus, and late-time decay behavior. The inclusion of deep images also supports source identification and the study of the surrounding field.

A key advantage of the system is its speed. When Swift observes a new GRB, the data are processed automatically and the online products are updated within minutes of their arrival. As additional observations are obtained, the light curves and associated products are refreshed, giving the community near-real-time access to the best available XRT data. This rapid availability is especially valuable for coordinating multi-wavelength follow-up observations, interpreting early afterglow behavior, and identifying unusual or scientifically important events.

By combining rapid processing, careful calibration, and uniform treatment of instrumental effects, the automated Swift/XRT GRB light-curve pipeline provides a reliable and accessible resource for the GRB community. It enables researchers to obtain publication-quality data products quickly, supports both immediate follow-up and archival studies, and ensures that observations from Swift/XRT can be used efficiently to advance our understanding of Gamma Ray Bursts and their afterglows.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an astronomy paper abstract about an online repository of Swift/XRT gamma-ray burst light curves, using the sections Context, Aims, Methods, and Results.
counterfactuals.output:
**Context.** The *Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory* has transformed the study of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) by providing rapid localizations and long-term X-ray follow-up with the X-Ray Telescope (XRT). The resulting X-ray afterglow light curves are central to investigations of GRB energetics, circumburst environments, emission mechanisms, and population properties. However, uniform access to reduced, calibrated, and consistently formatted XRT light-curve products is essential for reproducible statistical studies and rapid comparison with new events.

**Aims.** We present an online repository of Swift/XRT GRB light curves designed to provide the community with a homogeneous, searchable, and regularly updated data set. The repository aims to facilitate both single-event analysis and large-sample studies by collecting XRT temporal products, associated metadata, and basic derived quantities in a common framework.

**Methods.** The database is built from public Swift/XRT observations of GRB afterglows. Light curves are processed using standardized reduction procedures, including screening of event files, extraction of source and background counts, correction for instrumental effects, and conversion to flux where appropriate. Data products are organized by GRB name and include time-resolved count-rate and flux light curves, uncertainties, observing-mode information, and links to relevant auxiliary files. A web interface enables browsing, filtering, visualization, and downloading of individual or bulk data products.

**Results.** The repository provides a uniform collection of Swift/XRT GRB light curves spanning the mission lifetime, with products suitable for afterglow modeling, temporal classification, and population analyses. It enables rapid comparison of newly detected bursts with previous events and supports reproducible studies of X-ray afterglow behavior, including canonical steep-decay, plateau, and normal-decay phases. By offering open access to consistently processed XRT light curves and metadata, the repository serves as a practical resource for GRB follow-up programs and multiwavelength transient astronomy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a research project that creates publication-quality Swift XRT light curves for gamma-ray bursts, with headings for Context, Aims, Methods, and Results.
counterfactuals.output:
## Context

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic explosions in the universe, and their X-ray afterglows provide crucial information about the physics of relativistic jets, circumburst environments, and central engines. NASA’s *Swift* satellite, particularly its X-Ray Telescope (XRT), has observed large numbers of GRB afterglows. However, producing reliable, publication-quality XRT light curves requires careful calibration, correction for instrumental effects, and consistent treatment of different observing modes.

## Aims

The project aims to provide a standardized, automated system for generating high-quality Swift XRT light curves for GRBs. Its goals are to make XRT afterglow data rapidly available to the community, ensure that the light curves are scientifically reliable, and reduce the need for individual researchers to repeat complex data-reduction procedures. The project also seeks to support both rapid follow-up studies and long-term statistical analyses of GRB afterglows.

## Methods

The project processes Swift XRT observations using calibrated data-reduction pipelines. It accounts for key instrumental and observational effects, including pile-up, bad pixels, vignetting, exposure variations, and changes between XRT observing modes such as Windowed Timing and Photon Counting modes. Source and background regions are selected automatically, count rates are corrected, and where possible converted into fluxes using spectral information. The resulting light curves are checked for quality and made available through an online repository in formats suitable for direct use in publications.

## Results

The project delivers uniform, publication-ready XRT light curves for a large sample of Swift GRBs. These light curves capture the diverse behavior of GRB X-ray afterglows, including steep early declines, plateaus, flares, and late-time power-law decays. By providing consistent data products, the project has become a valuable resource for the GRB community, enabling rapid interpretation of individual bursts and broad comparative studies of afterglow populations.

We present an automated online database of gamma-ray burst (GRB) X-ray afterglows constructed from data obtained with the *Swift* X-Ray Telescope (XRT). The system ingests newly downlinked *Swift* observations, identifies GRB pointings, and processes the event data through a uniform analysis pipeline to produce calibrated X-ray light curves, hardness-ratio evolution, and stacked deep images of the burst fields. Source and background regions are selected automatically, with corrections applied for exposure variations, vignetting, bad columns, pile-up, and point-spread-function losses where required. Count-rate light curves are generated on adaptive time bins to preserve signal-to-noise, while hardness ratios are computed in standard soft and hard X-ray bands to trace spectral evolution during the prompt tail, steep decay, plateau, and late afterglow phases. Deep images are created by combining available XRT exposures to improve source localization and to search for faint late-time emission.

The database is designed for rapid response: once *Swift* telemetry becomes available, products are generated and posted to the web within minutes, providing the community with near-real-time access to homogeneous GRB X-ray data products. Each burst page includes quick-look plots, downloadable data tables, image products, and links to the underlying observations, enabling immediate follow-up planning as well as statistical studies of afterglow behavior. By applying a consistent reduction procedure to the full *Swift* GRB sample, the database provides a uniform resource for investigating X-ray temporal morphology, spectral evolution, energetics, and the connection between prompt and afterglow emission. This service supports both rapid multi-wavelength observing campaigns and long-term population studies of GRBs in the *Swift* era.
